claim: The literature we rest on must be work that mattered: papers a field is built on, results with large gains, and accounts from systems in real use that hit a limit and changed design (his example: Discord moving its message store between databases); small academic refinements are not what is asked for. A company's own figures are self-reported and are marked so.
when: Before choosing which sources a round reads, and before resting a design on a source.
quote: I want to be sure that you're looking at actual good papers, because like not just minimal improvement academic stuff, like actual published stuff.

claim: The library is to be filled properly, so that later sessions can use and reuse it and the work survives context compaction; and it can be poisoned, so a wrong record must be kept out: nothing enters without a source it can be checked against, and a lane reaches the board only after a check of its records.
when: Before writing records, before listing a lane or a file on the board, and when a child session reports records.
quote: we have to also make sure that you're populating the library properly so that it can be properly used, reused later as well.
note: He added: 'But we can poison the library as well, so keep that in mind.'

claim: Round 3 as it stands on 2026-11-19: the three first orchestrators (w1, c1, t1) stopped at their context ceilings and each lane was handed to a fresh Opus session from its state file (c1 at the fold, after 66 claims of which the refuter confirmed 41, narrowed 23 and refuted 2; w1 and t1 at the analysis); each lane got one more collector for accounts from systems in real use; a fourth lane, a1, was started on the two parts of the decision rule that still rest on reasoning alone: a token allowance that refills, and the scheduling of a few long units.
when: Before starting any of this research again: read the lanes' state files in docs/program/evidence/round3-2026-11-18/ first.
note: App session names: r3-check-2, r3-writers-2, r3-tree-2, r3-budget. Nothing of the round is checked by the top session yet; the verdict counts are c1's own report.

claim: In round 3 an Opus orchestrator session stood at about 114,000 tokens before its first helper returned (about 64,000 of fixed load plus the board, the README, the round's files, part of the orchestration document and its own briefs), passed 130,000 after its five collectors (148,250 and 158,600 in two lanes, 163,000 in the third), and reached about 177,000 after three steps; so under a ceiling of 130,000 one lane of six steps took two sessions. Three sessions, one day, one repository.
note: The successors were briefed to read only the state file and three sections of the round's file; whether that lets them finish in one session is not known yet.
